summary: Documents the RC4-HMAC Kerberos encryption types introduced by Microsoft in Windows 2000 as an alternative to the DES-based types, to ease upgrading from Windows NT environments. This RFC is historic.

eli5.summary: Windows 2000 used its own lock type for tickets, built from a scrambler called RC4. This note writes down how that lock works so others can match it. It is now historic.

questions: why did windows 2000 use rc4 for kerberos
what does fortybits mean in kerberos
subtitle: How Windows 2000 Kerberos used RC4 and HMAC-MD5 to encrypt tickets and messages.

tldr.problem: Windows 2000 needed Kerberos encryption that worked for upgraded Windows NT accounts, which had no DES keys, and that could be exported with a single product build.
tldr.mechanism: It defines two RC4-based encryption types and one HMAC-MD5 checksum type, with a key taken from the NT password hash and per-message key derivation based on the message type.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is now Historic and was updated by RFC 6649. It also advises against using these types for high-volume connections and where stronger types such as aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 are available.

today: RFC 4757 is Historic and was updated by RFC 6649. It was published as Informational, and the text itself recommends stronger encryption types when they are available.

sections.title: Why Windows Added New Types
sections.content:
This Informational RFC documents the RC4 Kerberos encryption types first introduced in Microsoft Windows 2000. The IESG note says they were published to describe a widely implemented technology, but they do not provide all operations of the Kerberos cryptography framework (RFC 3961), so they are not suitable for the standards track.

Windows 2000 added two encryption types and one checksum type for two reasons. 56-bit DES could not be exported early in development, and accounts upgraded from Windows NT 4.0 have no DES keying material. 3DES was also not exportable when Windows 2000 shipped, and there was a wish for one flavor of encryption for both US and international products.
sections.eli5: Windows had a problem: its old accounts did not have the right keys for the usual lock, and the usual lock could not be shipped everywhere. So it made a new lock.

sections.title: Keys from the NT Password Hash
sections.content:
For compatibility, the key used for RC4-HMAC is the same as the existing Windows NT key, the NT password hash. Once an account password is changed, DES-based keys are created and kept, and DES-based types can then be used.

The string-to-key function is K = MD4(UNICODE(password)). Each Windows Unicode character is encoded as 2 octets in little-endian order, and MD4 (RFC 1320) is computed over just those characters, without the terminating zero octets. The RFC gives the result for the password "foo" as a 16-octet value starting 0xac, 0x8e, 0x65, 0x7f.

Each message also gets its own key derivation. The message type T, a little-endian four-byte integer, is mixed into the keying material. For example, T is 1 for the AS-REQ encrypted timestamp, 2 for tickets, and 8 for the AS-REP encrypted part.
sections.eli5: The secret key is made by scrambling your password the same way old Windows already did, and every kind of message gets its own twist so keys are not reused.

sections.title: Checksum and Encryption Types
sections.content:
The checksum type is KERB_CHECKSUM_HMAC_MD5 (-138). It derives a signing key as Ksign = HMAC(K, "signaturekey"), hashes the message type and data with MD5, and computes an HMAC of that hash with Ksign.

The two encryption types are rc4-hmac (23) and rc4-hmac-exp (24, the exportable form). Encrypted data starts with a header of a 16-octet Checksum and an 8-octet Confounder. The sender derives keys with HMAC from the key and message type, fills the confounder with a pseudo-random number, computes the checksum with HMAC, and then encrypts the confounder and data with RC4. For the exportable type, part of the key is fixed to 0xAB bytes and the string "fortybits" is used. That name dates from when 40-bit keys were all that could be exported from the United States; the key size is actually 56 bits.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a random scrambling pattern and a tamper-proof stamp. The export version uses a weaker, shorter key to follow old shipping rules.

sections.title: Key Strength and GSS-API
sections.content:
A client and server using mutual authentication can negotiate key length. A client that cannot do full-strength encryption may propose a weaker key in the authenticator subkey field. The server then returns the same key or suggests its own in the AP reply. The two keys used for GSS-API message tokens are one of 128 bits and one of 56 bits.

The RFC also adapts the Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism (RFC 1964) to the new types. The sequence number is always sent in big-endian order, and the only supported quality of protection is GSS_KRB5_INTEG_C_QOP_DEFAULT (0x0). Windows 2000 defines three extra context flags: GSS_C_DCE_STYLE (0x1000), GSS_C_IDENTIFY_FLAG (0x2000) and GSS_C_EXTENDED_ERROR_FLAG (0x4000). They are used only by clients that know them, through the Windows Security Support Provider Interface. MIC and Wrap tokens use SGN_ALG 11 00 for HMAC and keep only the first 8 octets of the checksum.
sections.eli5: If one side can only handle a weaker lock, the two sides agree on a key that both can use. Windows also added a few extra switches for its own programs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because these types use a stream cipher, a different IV must be used in each direction with a session key or the encryption is weak. Using the sequence number as an IV avoids this. The RFC describes known attacks on RC4 that can leak information if the same data, such as a password, is encrypted in many separate keystreams. A new keystream is built for every message, but the RFC still RECOMMENDS not using these types for high-volume connections.

It also discusses weaknesses in MD4, including collisions found in August 2004. It argues the intended use does not rely on collision resistance and that MD4 is always keyed here, but notes that no study has proved HMAC-MD4 secure. It RECOMMENDS not using these types if stronger ones, such as aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96, are available.
sections.eli5: The authors say this lock has known weak spots, so if you have a stronger lock available, use that one instead.

items.label: KERB_CHECKSUM_HMAC_MD5
items.desc: The one checksum type, an HMAC over an MD5 hash.

items.label: KERB_ETYPE_RC4_HMAC_EXP
items.desc: Exportable form, with a key effectively 56 bits long.
